From Tomato Waste to Vegan Leather: How One Indian Startup Is Turning Agricultural By‑products Into Fashion Materials

02 Nov 2026, 04:09 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily World Desk · Source: timesofindia.indiatimes.com

Overview

A small‑scale experiment by biotechnology student Pritesh Mistry has grown into The Bio Company, a venture that converts discarded tomato skins and seeds into a plant‑based leather alternative called Bioleather. The company claims the material is free of polyurethane (PU) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC), biodegradable, and suitable for items such as handbags, shoes, and automotive interiors.

Confirmed facts from the Times of India report

  • Origin: The idea emerged while Mistry was studying at Thadomal Shahani Engineering College in Mumbai, after visits to leather tanneries and farms highlighted waste and pollution issues.
  • Technology: The process mixes tomato by‑products with biopolymers, plant‑based binders and natural fibres to produce a flexible sheet that mimics leather texture.
  • Recognition: The Bio Company won the *Best Innovation in Textile* award at the 2021 PETA Vegan Fashion Awards.
  • Production scale: A February 2025 report by *Tomato News* (cited in the Times of India article) states the firm produces roughly 5,000 metres of Bioleather per month at its current facility.
  • Commercial use: Toronto‑based label Satuhati began designing with Bioleather in 2024 and moved to limited commercial production a few months later.

Practical implications for designers and manufacturers

  • Material sourcing: Companies can source Bioleather from The Bio Company’s Mumbai‑area facility, which aggregates tomato waste from farms and processing units.
  • Design considerations: The sheet offers leather‑like flexibility but may differ in tensile strength; prototypes should be tested for the specific end‑use (e.g., handbags vs. automotive upholstery).
  • Environmental claims: Brands can market the product as vegan and PU/PVC‑free, but should disclose that a full environmental impact assessment is pending.
  • Supply chain stability: Since the feedstock depends on seasonal tomato harvests, manufacturers may need to plan inventory around peak waste periods or negotiate long‑term contracts with the supplier.

How to verify the announcement and product claims

  • Visit the company website – The Bio Company lists its material specifications, certifications, and contact details.
  • Request a material data sheet – Look for third‑party testing results on biodegradability, tensile strength, and chemical composition.
  • Check independent reports – Search for life‑cycle analyses or sustainability audits published by NGOs or academic institutions.
  • Contact the award organizers – The PETA Vegan Fashion Awards can confirm the 2021 award and any criteria used.
  • Cross‑reference production figures – Compare the 5,000 metres/month claim with any filings or trade data, if available.

Outlook

If the scaling challenges cited by Mistry—consistent waste supply and quality control—are addressed, tomato‑derived Bioleather could become a niche yet growing alternative to both animal leather and conventional synthetic leathers. Its success would illustrate a broader trend of circular agriculture, where food‑industry residues are repurposed into high‑value materials, potentially reducing landfill waste and the environmental footprint of fashion.
